conclusion.label: rejects

report:
### Conclusion
Claims that conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) supplements effectively reduce body or abdominal fat in humans are overstated. Although CLA significantly reduces fat mass in animal models, human clinical evidence demonstrates inconsistent, minimal, or non-existent effects.

### Summary of Evidence
* **Discrepancy Between Animal and Human Studies:** According to the National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements, while CLA reduces body fat in growing animals, human clinical trials demonstrate either no effect or only modest reductions in body weight or body fat compared to placebo [https://ods.od.nih.gov/pubs/conferences/cla.pdf].
* **High-Quality Trial Outcomes:** A systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis evaluating CLA supplementation on body composition noted that data specifically from high-quality studies failed to show body fat–lowering properties [https://nutrition-evidence.com/article/443152/the-effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-dose-response-meta-analysis].
* **Inconsistent Human Results:** A meta-analysis examining the efficacy of CLA as a dietary supplement highlights that while fat reduction in animal studies is consistent, human study results remain inconsistent [https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext].

### Sources

* https://nutrition-evidence.com/article/443152/the-effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-dose-response-meta-analysis
* https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext
